items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 6: Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk
items.why: The classification rule. High-risk means a safety component of a regulated product (Art. 6(1)) or a use listed in Annex III (Art. 6(2)). Art. 6(3) lets an Annex III system fall out where it poses no significant risk, but never where it profiles people; a provider relying on that must document the assessment (Art. 6(4)). New paragraphs 1a to 1c say systems used solely for non-safety aspects such as user assistance or performance optimisation are not safety components, unless their failure would endanger health and safety. The Act's operative text does not use the labels 'limited risk' or 'minimal risk'. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Annex III: High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2)
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Annex III, points 1 to 8; point 3 (education), point 4(a) (recruitment), point 5(b) (credit)
items.quote: AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons
items.why: The list a classification method has to be tested against: eight areas, from biometrics to the administration of justice. Each entry turns on what the system is 'intended to be used' for, which is why the same technology can sit in different classes. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 5: Prohibited AI practices
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Art. 5(1)(a)-(h); points (ba) and (bb) and paragraphs 1a and 1b marked NEW
items.quote: The following AI practices shall be prohibited:
items.why: The top class. Covers manipulation, exploitation of vulnerability, social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion inference at work and in education, and others. Two prohibitions added by the Digital Omnibus concern non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 113: Entry into force and application
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Art. 113, third paragraph, points (a) and (c), both marked AMENDED
items.why: Source of the dates in the brief: Chapters I and II (including the prohibitions) from 2 February 2025; the two new prohibitions from 2 December 2026. Also read: high-risk rules from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I products). The page footer still says the tool uses the 'Official version of 13 June 2024', which conflicts with the banner; the banner and the AMENDED markers were relied on. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 2: Scope
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union
items.why: Why a UK organisation classifies against the EU classes at all: the Act applies to providers and deployers in a third country where the system's output is used in the Union. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (white paper)
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: We will not assign rules or risk levels to entire sectors or technologies.
items.why: Source of the quotation and of the UK position: regulation by context and outcome, with no statutory tiers. The page shows 'Updated 3 August 2023' and a notice that it was published under the 2022 to 2024 government; no later statement replacing this approach was read in this pass.

items.title: SS1/23 Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Principle 1.3 'Model tiering', points (a)-(e), PDF p.12-13; Principle 1.2 'Model inventory'; paragraphs 1.2-1.3 (scope) and 1.5 (effective date)
items.quote: Firms should implement a consistent, firm-wide model tiering approach
items.why: The nearest UK regulatory expectation of tiering: a materiality and complexity rating for each model, the approach periodically validated, individual tier assignments independently reassessed. Covers models developed in-house or externally, including vendor models. Applies only to banks, building societies and designated investment firms with internal model approval; in effect from 17 May 2024. Not written for AI alone, though complexity factors include explainability and bias.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in UK financial services - 2024
items.publisher: Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority
items.quote: 62% of all AI use cases are rated low materiality by the firms that use them with 16% rated high materiality
items.why: Source of the figures: a third of AI use cases are third-party implementations (17% in the 2022 survey); 62% rated low materiality and 16% high; 118 responses. Limits: regulated financial firms only, self-reported, and 'materiality' is the firms' own rating, not an AI Act class.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Section 1.2.3 'Risk Prioritization', p.7; MAP 4.1 and 4.2, Table 2, p.27; GOVERN 6.1, Table 1, p.24
items.quote: Policies and resources should be prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system.
items.why: International comparator. Supports tiering as a way to direct effort, and asks for the risks of third-party components to be mapped and documented. Voluntary, United States.

items.title: International AI Safety Report 2026
items.publisher: International AI Safety Report (chair: Yoshua Bengio)
items.locator: Executive summary, 'Real-world evidence for several risks is growing'; chapter 2 introduction; section 3.2, Table 3.1 and 'Risk thresholds/risk tiers'
items.quote: General-purpose AI risks fall into three categories: malicious use, malfunctions, and systemic risks.
items.why: A taxonomy for the identification half of the question. Covers general-purpose AI at the frontier, not ordinary business tools, and is descriptive, not a standard. Read on the report's own site; the gov.uk address tried for the 2026 report returned 404.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 35: Data protection impact assessment
items.quote: a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons which is based on automated processing, including profiling
items.why: The one risk screen UK statute does apply to AI that handles personal data: processing 'likely to result in a high risk' must be assessed first, and Art. 35(3) names three cases where that is always so, the first being automated evaluation and profiling on which significant decisions are based. A two-level screen for personal data processing, not a set of AI tiers; it says nothing about systems that use no personal data.

items.title: Data protection impact assessments: When do we need to do a DPIA?
items.locator: Section 'What does 'likely to result in a high risk' mean?'; section 'What does the ICO consider likely to result in high risk?' (innovative technology, denial of service)
items.quote: are there features which point to the potential for high risk?
items.why: The regulator's method for sorting processing into high risk or not: a high-level screen for red flags, with a published list under Art. 35(4). Use of innovative technology, AI included, needs an assessment when combined with another listed factor. Marked under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. No date printed on the page; the year given is the year it was read.

items.title: Use of artificial intelligence in government (HC 612, Session 2023-24)
items.quote: Only 30% of all 87 survey respondents reported that they had risk and quality assurance processes that explicitly incorporated AI risks
items.why: Audit evidence on how far risk identification has got in practice. The same paragraph reports that almost half of the 32 bodies with deployed AI (15) kept no register of live AI use cases, so had nothing to classify. Limits: central government bodies only, self-reported survey (position as at autumn 2023), and a further 46% said they planned such processes.

items.title: General principles for classification of high-risk AI systems (summary of the draft Commission guidelines)
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: Check whether the AI system falls within one of the high-risk use cases in the sensitive areas listed in Annex III.
items.why: The Commission's own six-step order for classifying a system: is it an AI system, what is its intended purpose, the Annex I route, the Annex III route, the Article 6(3) filter, and any transitional rule. A summary of DRAFT guidelines under Article 6(5): the Commission's library page dates the draft 19 May 2026 and the Service Desk still describes it as open to consultation until 23 July 2026, before formal adoption. Not binding, and may change on adoption. No date printed on this page.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 7: Amendments to Annex III
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: to amend Annex III by adding or modifying use-cases of high-risk AI systems where both of the following conditions are fulfilled
items.why: Why a classification cannot be done once and filed: the Commission may add or modify high-risk use cases by delegated act where a system in a listed area poses a risk equal to or greater than those already listed. This is the change a board would need to see coming, which is what the top level of the question asks. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

items.title: AI Risk Assessment: A Scenario-Based, Proportional Methodology for the AI Act
items.publisher: Digital Society (Springer Nature); C. Novelli, F. Casolari, A. Rotolo, M. Taddeo and L. Floridi
items.quote: However, it lacks a clear methodology for the assessment of these risks in concrete situations.
items.why: Peer-reviewed, open access. Argues that the AI Act's classes rest on broad application areas and so can misjudge the risk of a system in a particular setting, and proposes assessing risk by scenario (hazard, exposure, vulnerability, response). Supports recording reasons for a tier and not only the label. A proposal, not an empirical test; written against the text as it stood before the 2026 amendments.

items.title: The AI risk repository: A meta-review, database, and taxonomy of risks from artificial intelligence
items.publisher: arXiv (P. Slattery, A. K. Saeri, E. A. C. Grundy and others); stated on the page as published in Patterns (Cell Press), 2026
items.quote: We systematically analyzed every major AI risk framework published to date-74 frameworks containing 1,725 distinct risks-and organized them into a unified system.
items.why: A meta-review for the identification half of the question: the abstract reports 74 frameworks and 1,725 risks sorted by cause and by domain, and attributes 38% of risks to human decisions against 42% to the AI system. Useful as a checklist of what a classification method should have looked for. Authors' repository copy; the arXiv page says the paper has since been published in Patterns. Only the abstract page was read. The counts are of risks named in frameworks, not of incidents.

items.title: OECD Framework for the Classification of AI Systems (OECD Digital Economy Papers No. 323)
items.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
items.locator: Executive summary, 'Key dimensions structure AI system characteristics and interactions'; Box 5 'AI risk-based approaches' (p.67)
items.quote: The framework classifies AI systems and applications along the following dimensions
items.why: International comparator. Classifies a system in its context of use along five dimensions (People & Planet, Economic Context, Data & Input, AI Model, Task & Output), which is a way to describe a bought-in tool before assigning it a tier. A descriptive policy tool, not a risk rating and not binding; it pre-dates general-purpose AI in wide use.

items.title: NSW AI Assessment Framework
items.locator: Opening section; notice 'The AIAF Platform is mandatory from 30 September 2026'
items.quote: AI systems assessed as high or critical risk must be submitted to the AI Secretariat
items.why: International comparator for the top level of the question: a government that requires every AI use case to be registered and risk-assessed, including procured systems, and sends the high and critical tiers to an independent review committee. New South Wales public sector only, under Circular DCS-2026-02; a self-assessment at the first stage. No date printed on the page.
